questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Geography?
options: The study of the Earth, people, places, and their relationships
The study of only ancient written records
The study of money management in firms
The study of chemical reactions in laboratories
questions.correctAnswer: The study of the Earth, people, places, and their relationships
questions.explanation: Geography explains natural features, human activities, places, and how people interact with environments.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe Geography as the study of the Earth and human-environment relationships.

questions.prompt: Which branch of Geography studies landforms, climate, soils, vegetation, and water bodies?
options: Physical Geography
Political History
Bookkeeping
Fine Art
questions.correctAnswer: Physical Geography
questions.explanation: Physical Geography focuses on natural features and processes on the Earth's surface.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify the main branches of Geography and their areas of study.

questions.prompt: A learner studies how Nairobi's population growth affects transport and housing. Which branch is most relevant?
options: Human Geography
Petrology
Astronomy
Organic Chemistry
questions.correctAnswer: Human Geography
questions.explanation: Human Geography studies people, settlements, economic activities, movement, and their effects on places.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate branches of Geography to real-life issues in Kenya.

questions.prompt: Which career most directly uses skills in map making and spatial data display?
options: Cartography
Welding
Pharmacy
Acting
questions.correctAnswer: Cartography
questions.explanation: Cartography is the science and skill of making maps that show spatial information clearly.
questions.learningOutcome: Connect Geography skills to career pathways.

questions.prompt: Why is Geography useful when planning a school tree-planting project?
options: It helps select suitable sites using soil, slope, climate, and land-use information
It replaces the need to water seedlings after planting
It proves that all trees grow equally well in every place
It only teaches names of countries and capitals
questions.correctAnswer: It helps select suitable sites using soil, slope, climate, and land-use information
questions.explanation: Geographical knowledge supports practical environmental decisions by comparing site conditions.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply geographical knowledge to local environmental action.

questions.prompt: Which pairing best shows the relationship between Geography and another learning area?
options: Geography and Mathematics: calculating gradients, averages, and map scales
Geography and Music: naming notes in a song
Geography and Literature: identifying rhyme patterns only
Geography and Business: avoiding all data and maps
questions.correctAnswer: Geography and Mathematics: calculating gradients, averages, and map scales
questions.explanation: Geography often uses mathematical skills to measure distance, gradient, area, and statistical patterns.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze links between Geography and other disciplines.

questions.prompt: A county wants to reduce flood losses near a river. Which Geography-based plan is most suitable?
options: Map flood-prone areas, regulate risky settlement, conserve wetlands, and improve warning systems
Build houses on the lowest river banks to shorten walking distance
Remove all river vegetation so water moves faster everywhere
Ignore rainfall data and wait for floods before acting
questions.correctAnswer: Map flood-prone areas, regulate risky settlement, conserve wetlands, and improve warning systems
questions.explanation: A strong geographical plan combines spatial mapping, land-use control, ecosystem protection, and preparedness.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate geographical approaches to solving community environmental problems.

questions.prompt: On a map, what does a scale of 1:50,000 mean?
options: 1 cm on the map represents 50,000 cm on the ground
1 cm on the map represents 50,000 km on the ground
50,000 cm on the map represents 1 cm on the ground
The map shows 50,000 towns
questions.correctAnswer: 1 cm on the map represents 50,000 cm on the ground
questions.explanation: A representative fraction compares map distance with the same unit distance on the ground.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret representative fraction map scales.

questions.prompt: A straight road measures 6 cm on a 1:50,000 map. What is its ground distance?
options: 3 km
30 km
0.3 km
questions.correctAnswer: 3 km
questions.explanation: At 1:50,000, 1 cm represents 0.5 km, so 6 cm represents 3 km.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate ground distance from map scale.

questions.prompt: Which map symbol is commonly shown using closely spaced brown lines to represent steep slopes?
options: Contour lines
Railway lines
County boundaries
Spot heights only
questions.correctAnswer: Contour lines
questions.explanation: Contour lines join places of equal height and their spacing helps show the steepness of slopes.
questions.learningOutcome: Use contour patterns to describe relief.

questions.prompt: If contours are close together on one side of a hill and far apart on another, what does this show?
options: One side is steep and the other side is gentle
The hill has no change in height
The map has no scale
The hill is under the sea
questions.correctAnswer: One side is steep and the other side is gentle
questions.explanation: Close contours show a rapid height change, while widely spaced contours show a gentler slope.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret relief from contour spacing.

questions.prompt: Which feature is usually shown by blue lines on a topographical map?
options: Rivers and streams
Main roads
Forest boundaries
Electric power lines
questions.correctAnswer: Rivers and streams
questions.explanation: Conventional map colours commonly use blue for water features such as rivers, streams, lakes, and swamps.
questions.learningOutcome: Recognize conventional symbols and colours on maps.

questions.prompt: A river flows from contours marked 1800 m to contours marked 1600 m. What direction is the river generally flowing?
options: From higher land toward lower land
From lower land toward higher land
Across the map without following relief
Only toward the map title
questions.correctAnswer: From higher land toward lower land
questions.explanation: Rivers flow downhill, so contour heights help identify the direction of flow.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze contour heights to infer drainage direction.

questions.prompt: Which evidence on a topographical map best suggests a nucleated settlement?
options: Many houses clustered around a road junction or market
Houses evenly scattered across farms
No buildings shown anywhere
Only contour lines and rivers
questions.correctAnswer: Many houses clustered around a road junction or market
questions.explanation: A nucleated settlement has buildings grouped closely, often near services, transport routes, or trading centres.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret settlement patterns from map evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the six-figure grid reference used for on a map?
options: Locating a feature more precisely within a grid square
Showing the age of a rock
Measuring rainfall for a whole year
Naming every road on the map
questions.correctAnswer: Locating a feature more precisely within a grid square
questions.explanation: Six-figure grid references divide a grid square into tenths to give a more precise location.
questions.learningOutcome: Use grid references to locate features on topographical maps.

questions.prompt: Which rule helps when reading eastings and northings on a grid map?
options: Read eastings first, then northings
Read northings first, then eastings
Ignore the grid numbers
Read only the largest number on the map
questions.correctAnswer: Read eastings first, then northings
questions.explanation: Grid references are read along the eastings first and then up the northings.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply the correct order when reading grid references.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to compare two routes from a village to a health centre. Which map-based factor is most important for choosing the easier walking route?
options: Distance, slope, river crossings, and road type
The colour of the map cover only
The number of letters in the village name
The position of the publisher's logo
questions.correctAnswer: Distance, slope, river crossings, and road type
questions.explanation: A practical route choice uses several map clues, including distance, relief, drainage, and transport features.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate map evidence to select a suitable route.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a gentle slope on a contour map?
options: Contours are widely spaced
Contours cross each other many times
Contours are absent from all highland areas
Contours are drawn in blue only
questions.correctAnswer: Contours are widely spaced
questions.explanation: Wide spacing between contours shows a gradual change in height over a longer horizontal distance.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe slopes using contour spacing.

questions.prompt: A map shows tea factories near high rainfall areas and transport routes. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: The industry is located near raw materials and routes to move processed tea
The factories are placed randomly without site advantages
Tea processing does not need roads or farms
The map only shows climate and cannot show economic activity
questions.correctAnswer: The industry is located near raw materials and routes to move processed tea
questions.explanation: Map interpretation connects land use, climate, raw materials, and transport to explain location patterns.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze relationships between map features and economic activities.

questions.prompt: A school fieldwork team must map land use around a market centre. Which method would give the most reliable map?
options: Use a base map, observe each plot, record coordinates, and confirm features with local checks
Guess land use from memory without visiting the area
Copy another town's land-use map
Use only one photograph taken indoors
questions.correctAnswer: Use a base map, observe each plot, record coordinates, and confirm features with local checks
questions.explanation: Reliable field mapping combines direct observation, location records, and verification of features.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a sound approach for collecting and mapping land-use data.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of the rainfall values 20 mm, 30 mm, and 40 mm?
options: 30 mm
20 mm
40 mm
90 mm
questions.correctAnswer: 30 mm
questions.explanation: The mean is found by adding the values and dividing by the number of values: 90 divided by 3 is 30.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate simple averages from geographical data.

questions.prompt: Which graph is most suitable for showing monthly rainfall totals for one weather station?
options: Bar graph
Sketch map
Flow diagram
Contour map
questions.correctAnswer: Bar graph
questions.explanation: A bar graph clearly compares separate monthly totals such as rainfall amounts.
questions.learningOutcome: Select suitable graphs for presenting geographical data.

questions.prompt: Which graph best shows how temperature changes from January to December?
options: Line graph
Dot map
Divided rectangle only
Wind rose
questions.correctAnswer: Line graph
questions.explanation: A line graph is useful for showing continuous change over time.
questions.learningOutcome: Choose a graph type for time-series geographical data.

questions.prompt: A class records the number of shops, schools, clinics, and farms in a village. Which method best shows their proportions?
options: Pie chart
Cross-section only
Contour diagram
Compass bearing
questions.correctAnswer: Pie chart
questions.explanation: A pie chart shows how parts make up a whole, so it can compare proportions of land-use categories.
questions.learningOutcome: Represent proportional geographical data using appropriate diagrams.

questions.prompt: What is the range of these daily temperatures: 18 C, 22 C, 25 C, and 30 C?
questions.explanation: The range is the highest value minus the lowest value: 30 minus 18 is 12.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate range from geographical data.

questions.prompt: A rainfall graph has no title, units, or labelled axes. What is the main weakness?
options: Readers cannot clearly know what data is shown or measured
The bars will automatically become too high
The data changes from rainfall to population
The graph can no longer be drawn on paper
questions.correctAnswer: Readers cannot clearly know what data is shown or measured
questions.explanation: Good graphs need titles, labels, and units so users can interpret data accurately.
questions.learningOutcome: Assess the quality of geographical data presentation.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to compare rainfall reliability in two counties over ten years. Which statistic is most useful in addition to the mean?
options: Range or variation from year to year
Number of letters in each county name
Height of the school flagpole
Distance from the classroom door
questions.correctAnswer: Range or variation from year to year
questions.explanation: The mean alone can hide differences in reliability, so variation helps compare consistency of rainfall.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate statistics needed to compare geographical patterns.

questions.prompt: In a class survey, 12 learners walk to school, 8 use bicycles, and 20 use public transport. What is the total sample size?
options: 40 learners
20 learners
12 learners
8 learners
questions.correctAnswer: 40 learners
questions.explanation: The sample size is the sum of all responses: 12 plus 8 plus 20 equals 40.
questions.learningOutcome: Summarize fieldwork data using simple totals.

questions.prompt: Why should a Geography report state the source of its rainfall data?
options: To help readers judge reliability and trace the data
To make the report longer without adding meaning
To replace the need for calculations
To hide where the information came from
questions.correctAnswer: To help readers judge reliability and trace the data
questions.explanation: Stating sources supports transparency and helps readers assess the quality of evidence.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the importance of reliable data sources in Geography.

questions.prompt: What does GIS stand for in Geography?
options: Geographic Information System
General Industry Survey
Ground Irrigation Scheme
Global Income Statement
questions.correctAnswer: Geographic Information System
questions.explanation: GIS is a computer-based system for capturing, storing, analyzing, and displaying location data.
questions.learningOutcome: Define GIS and its role in Geography.

questions.prompt: Which GIS layer would best show the location of schools in a sub-county?
options: Point layer
Temperature line graph
Rock cycle diagram
Rain gauge cylinder
questions.correctAnswer: Point layer
questions.explanation: Schools can be represented as points because each school has a specific location.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify GIS data types used for different features.

questions.prompt: Which device is commonly used to collect coordinates during fieldwork?
options: GPS receiver or smartphone with location service
Barometer only
Microscope only
Bunsen burner
questions.correctAnswer: GPS receiver or smartphone with location service
questions.explanation: GPS-enabled devices use satellites to estimate position coordinates on the Earth's surface.
questions.learningOutcome: Use location technology to support geographical fieldwork.

questions.prompt: A GIS map has layers for rivers, roads, schools, and population density. What is the advantage of using layers?
options: Different types of information can be viewed together or separately
All information is erased after one map view
Layers prevent users from comparing places
Layers make coordinates unnecessary in all cases
questions.correctAnswer: Different types of information can be viewed together or separately
questions.explanation: GIS layers allow users to overlay and compare spatial information for better analysis.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain how GIS layers support spatial analysis.

questions.prompt: A county health team maps clinics and villages to identify underserved areas. Which GIS operation is most useful?
options: Overlaying clinic locations with population distribution
Changing all map labels to the same colour
Deleting village data before analysis
Using rainfall data only for all decisions
questions.correctAnswer: Overlaying clinic locations with population distribution
questions.explanation: Overlaying layers helps compare service locations with where people live.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze GIS layers to support planning decisions.

questions.prompt: Which GIS workflow would best support planning evacuation routes in a flood-prone town?
options: Combine flood-risk zones, roads, bridges, high ground, and population data to identify safe routes
Map only restaurants and ignore roads and flood levels
Use last year's exam timetable as the main layer
Place all evacuation centres inside the deepest floodplain
questions.correctAnswer: Combine flood-risk zones, roads, bridges, high ground, and population data to identify safe routes
questions.explanation: Emergency planning needs several spatial layers so routes avoid danger and reach people efficiently.
questions.learningOutcome: Create a GIS-based approach for solving a local hazard-planning problem.

questions.prompt: Which type of rock forms when molten material cools and solidifies?
options: Igneous rock
Sedimentary rock
Metamorphic rock
Alluvial soil
questions.correctAnswer: Igneous rock
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks form from cooled magma below the surface or lava at the surface.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify rock types by their mode of formation.

questions.prompt: Which rock type is formed from compacted and cemented sediments?
options: Sedimentary rock
Intrusive igneous rock
Metamorphic rock
Basalt only
questions.correctAnswer: Sedimentary rock
questions.explanation: Sedimentary rocks form when sediments are deposited, compressed, and cemented over time.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe how sedimentary rocks form.

questions.prompt: Which rock is a common example of a metamorphic rock?
options: Marble
Pumice
Conglomerate
Shale
questions.correctAnswer: Marble
questions.explanation: Marble forms when limestone is changed by heat and pressure.
questions.learningOutcome: Give examples of rocks formed by metamorphism.

questions.prompt: Why does basalt usually have smaller crystals than granite?
options: Basalt cools quickly at or near the surface
Basalt is always older than granite
Granite forms only from cemented sand
Basalt is made from plant remains
questions.correctAnswer: Basalt cools quickly at or near the surface
questions.explanation: Fast cooling gives crystals little time to grow, while slow cooling underground forms larger crystals.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate cooling rate to crystal size in igneous rocks.

questions.prompt: Which process changes limestone into marble?
options: Heat and pressure during metamorphism
Evaporation of seawater only
Freezing of lava at the surface
Wind transport of sand grains
questions.correctAnswer: Heat and pressure during metamorphism
questions.explanation: Metamorphism alters existing rocks through heat, pressure, or chemically active fluids.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain conditions that lead to metamorphic rock formation.

questions.prompt: Which use of limestone is important in Kenya's construction industry?
options: Making cement
Making petrol
Generating tidal power
Producing cotton fibre
questions.correctAnswer: Making cement
questions.explanation: Limestone is a key raw material for cement manufacturing, including in areas near Athi River and Bamburi.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate rocks and minerals to economic uses in Kenya.

questions.prompt: A rock sample contains visible layers and small fossils. Which conclusion is most likely?
options: It is sedimentary and formed from deposited materials
It is fresh lava from an active eruption
It formed only inside a deep fault by melting
It is a man-made plastic material
questions.correctAnswer: It is sedimentary and formed from deposited materials
questions.explanation: Layering and fossils are common clues of sedimentary origin.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze rock characteristics to infer origin.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best represents one possible path in the rock cycle?
options: Magma cools into igneous rock, weathering produces sediments, sediments form sedimentary rock
Sediments melt into ice, ice becomes coal, coal becomes rainfall
Lava becomes a plant, the plant becomes granite, granite becomes wind
Limestone grows crystals, crystals turn into sunlight, sunlight becomes shale
questions.correctAnswer: Magma cools into igneous rock, weathering produces sediments, sediments form sedimentary rock
questions.explanation: The rock cycle links rock formation, weathering, erosion, deposition, and changes by heat or pressure.
questions.learningOutcome: Synthesize processes in the rock cycle.

questions.prompt: Why are rocks important in soil formation?
options: Weathering breaks rocks into mineral particles that mix with organic matter
Rocks prevent all plants from growing anywhere
Rocks turn directly into rain clouds every afternoon
Rocks remove all nutrients from every soil
questions.correctAnswer: Weathering breaks rocks into mineral particles that mix with organic matter
questions.explanation: Parent rock materials influence soil texture, mineral content, and fertility after weathering.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze the role of rocks in soil development.

questions.prompt: Which fieldwork activity best helps learners classify rocks in a local area?
options: Observe texture, colour, hardness, layers, and mineral grains, then record sample locations
Collect rocks randomly and throw away all field notes
Classify rocks only by the learner's favourite colour
Use rainfall totals without inspecting any rock sample
questions.correctAnswer: Observe texture, colour, hardness, layers, and mineral grains, then record sample locations
questions.explanation: Rock classification needs observable properties and accurate field records.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply field observation skills to rock classification.

questions.prompt: What is tectonic plate movement mainly responsible for?
options: Earthquakes, folding, faulting, and vulcanicity
Daily sunrise and sunset
Photosynthesis in crops
Formation of bank accounts
questions.correctAnswer: Earthquakes, folding, faulting, and vulcanicity
questions.explanation: Movement of plates creates forces that deform rocks, trigger earthquakes, and support volcanic activity.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify effects of tectonic plate movement.

questions.prompt: Which force is mainly associated with crustal compression?
options: Forces pushing rock layers together
Forces pulling rock layers apart only
Evaporation from lakes
Condensation in clouds
questions.correctAnswer: Forces pushing rock layers together
questions.explanation: Compression squeezes rock layers and can produce folding or reverse faulting.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe forces involved in earth movements.

questions.prompt: Which feature is most closely linked to tensional forces in the crust?
options: Rift valley
River meander
Sand dune
Coral reef
questions.correctAnswer: Rift valley
questions.explanation: Tensional forces can pull the crust apart, causing faulting and formation of rift valleys.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate crustal forces to landform development.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why parts of the East African Rift have volcanic and earthquake activity?
options: The crust is being stretched, creating faults and pathways for magma
The region has no movement in the Earth's crust
All rivers in the area flow uphill
The area is far from all tectonic influence
questions.correctAnswer: The crust is being stretched, creating faults and pathways for magma
questions.explanation: Rifting is linked to extension, faulting, earthquakes, and volcanic activity in parts of eastern Africa.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply plate movement ideas to East African Rift examples.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows rock layers bent but not broken. Which process is most likely shown?
options: Folding caused by compressional forces
Chemical weathering by rainwater only
Deposition of river alluvium
Mass wasting on a steep slope
questions.correctAnswer: Folding caused by compressional forces
questions.explanation: When rocks bend under pressure without breaking, the structure is a fold.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze diagrams of crustal deformation.

questions.prompt: A town is built near an active fault. Which planning approach best reduces risk from earth movements?
options: Map fault zones, enforce safe building standards, prepare evacuation plans, and educate residents
Build the tallest buildings directly on the fault trace
Remove all open spaces to increase crowding
Ignore small tremors because they never indicate risk
questions.correctAnswer: Map fault zones, enforce safe building standards, prepare evacuation plans, and educate residents
questions.explanation: Risk reduction combines hazard mapping, safer construction, preparedness, and public awareness.
questions.learningOutcome: Develop risk-reduction strategies for areas affected by earth movements.

questions.prompt: What is an anticline?
options: An upfold in rock layers
A downfold in rock layers
A vertical volcanic pipe
A flat coastal plain
questions.correctAnswer: An upfold in rock layers
questions.explanation: An anticline is an arch-like fold where rock layers bend upward.
questions.learningOutcome: Define basic fold structures.

questions.prompt: What is a syncline?
options: A downfold in rock layers
A lava plateau
A river cliff
A sand bar
questions.correctAnswer: A downfold in rock layers
questions.explanation: A syncline is a trough-like fold where rock layers bend downward.
questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish anticlines from synclines.

questions.prompt: Which condition makes folding more likely than faulting?
options: Rock layers are compressed slowly and are warm or flexible enough to bend
Rock layers are pulled apart suddenly and are very brittle
Water evaporates from a lake surface
Wind deposits sand in a desert
questions.correctAnswer: Rock layers are compressed slowly and are warm or flexible enough to bend
questions.explanation: Slow compression under suitable pressure and temperature allows rocks to bend into folds.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain conditions that favour folding.

questions.prompt: Which mountain range is a well-known example of young fold mountains?
options: Himalayas
Aberdare Range
Mount Longonot
Yatta Plateau
questions.correctAnswer: Himalayas
questions.explanation: The Himalayas formed from powerful compressional forces where tectonic plates converged.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify examples of fold mountains.

questions.prompt: Which land-use advantage can folded landscapes provide?
options: Valleys may provide routes and settlements while ridges can form grazing or forest areas
All folded areas are flat and identical
Folded landscapes have no soils or water sources
Folds prevent every form of transport
questions.correctAnswer: Valleys may provide routes and settlements while ridges can form grazing or forest areas
questions.explanation: Folded relief creates varied slopes, ridges, and valleys that influence transport, settlement, and land use.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze how folded landscapes influence human activities.

questions.prompt: A cross-section shows one limb of a fold pushed over the other. Which term best fits this feature?
options: Overfold
Simple symmetrical fold
Delta
Barchan dune
questions.correctAnswer: Overfold
questions.explanation: An overfold forms when one limb is pushed beyond the vertical due to strong compression.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret types of folds from cross-section diagrams.

questions.prompt: Which investigation would best help learners explain folding in a classroom model?
options: Push layered soft material from both sides and compare the folds with labelled diagrams
Pour water over a flat floor and call the puddles folds
Heat sand until it changes colour and ignore layers
Draw only a map title without showing rock layers
questions.correctAnswer: Push layered soft material from both sides and compare the folds with labelled diagrams
questions.explanation: A model with layered material and compression demonstrates how folding can occur in rock layers.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a simple model to demonstrate folding processes.

questions.prompt: What is vulcanicity?
options: The movement of magma within or onto the Earth's crust
The daily change from day to night
The growth of crops in highlands
The recording of census data
questions.correctAnswer: The movement of magma within or onto the Earth's crust
questions.explanation: Vulcanicity includes both underground movement of magma and surface volcanic eruptions.
questions.learningOutcome: Define vulcanicity and its basic processes.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between magma and lava?
options: Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is molten rock at the surface
Magma is rainwater; lava is groundwater
Magma is always solid; lava is always gas
Magma forms only from plants; lava forms only from animals
questions.correctAnswer: Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is molten rock at the surface
questions.explanation: The name changes from magma to lava when molten rock reaches the Earth's surface.
questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish magma from lava.

questions.prompt: Which feature forms when magma cools in a vertical crack?
options: Dyke
Lava flow
Crater lake
River delta
questions.correctAnswer: Dyke
questions.explanation: A dyke is a vertical or steeply inclined sheet of igneous rock formed in a crack.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify intrusive volcanic features.

questions.prompt: Which volcanic feature is a broad depression formed after a major eruption or collapse of a volcano?
options: Caldera
Levee
Meander
Interfluve
questions.correctAnswer: Caldera
questions.explanation: A caldera is a large volcanic depression, often formed when a magma chamber empties and the surface collapses.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe major extrusive volcanic landforms.

questions.prompt: Why do some volcanic areas in Kenya have fertile soils?
options: Weathered volcanic rocks can release minerals into the soil
Lava removes every nutrient permanently
Volcanic ash is always poisonous to all crops forever
Volcanic areas never receive rainfall
questions.correctAnswer: Weathered volcanic rocks can release minerals into the soil
questions.explanation: Over time, volcanic materials can weather into mineral-rich soils that support farming.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain positive effects of vulcanicity on human activities.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would suggest that an area has experienced past volcanic activity?
options: Lava flows, volcanic cones, crater lakes, and geothermal steam vents
Only straight tarmac roads and road signs
Only school buildings and playing fields
Only printed population tables
questions.correctAnswer: Lava flows, volcanic cones, crater lakes, and geothermal steam vents
questions.explanation: Volcanic landscapes often contain cones, craters, lava flows, hot springs, and geothermal features.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze landscape evidence of volcanic activity.

questions.prompt: A settlement lies on the lower slope of a dormant volcano. Which hazard should planners consider?
options: Possible lava flows, ash fall, landslides, or gas emissions if activity resumes
Permanent protection from all natural hazards
No need for water supply planning
Complete absence of slope-related risk
questions.correctAnswer: Possible lava flows, ash fall, landslides, or gas emissions if activity resumes
questions.explanation: Volcanic slopes can expose people to eruption hazards and slope instability.
questions.learningOutcome: Assess volcanic hazards for settlement planning.

questions.prompt: Which plan best balances the benefits and risks of using a volcanic landscape?
options: Use fertile soils and geothermal resources while zoning high-risk slopes and monitoring hazards
Ban all farming, energy production, and tourism from every volcanic area
Build dense settlements inside all craters without monitoring
Ignore scientific data because volcanic landscapes never change
questions.correctAnswer: Use fertile soils and geothermal resources while zoning high-risk slopes and monitoring hazards
questions.explanation: Sustainable use of volcanic areas should combine economic benefits with hazard awareness and land-use control.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate sustainable land use in volcanic regions.

questions.prompt: Which Kenyan area is well known for geothermal power linked to volcanic activity?
options: Olkaria near Naivasha
Lamu old town shoreline
Kakamega Forest canopy
Lake Victoria beaches
questions.correctAnswer: Olkaria near Naivasha
questions.explanation: Olkaria lies in the Rift Valley and uses geothermal steam associated with volcanic heat.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify Kenyan examples of volcanic resources.

questions.prompt: What is the focus of an earthquake?
options: The point inside the Earth where seismic energy is released
The point on the surface directly above every cloud
The highest point of a fold mountain
The mouth of a river
questions.correctAnswer: The point inside the Earth where seismic energy is released
questions.explanation: The focus is the underground point where an earthquake starts.
questions.learningOutcome: Define basic earthquake terms.

questions.prompt: What is the epicentre of an earthquake?
options: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus
The deepest part of the ocean floor only
The centre of a river meander
The highest contour on any map
questions.correctAnswer: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus
questions.explanation: The epicentre lies on the surface above the focus and often experiences strong shaking.
questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish earthquake focus from epicentre.

questions.prompt: Which instrument records earthquake waves?
options: Seismograph
Rain gauge
Anemometer
Hygrometer
questions.correctAnswer: Seismograph
questions.explanation: A seismograph records seismic waves produced by earthquakes.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify instruments used to study earthquakes.

questions.prompt: Which action is safest during strong earthquake shaking inside a classroom?
options: Drop, cover under a sturdy desk, and hold on until shaking stops
Run to the windows and lean on the glass
Use the lift immediately
Stand under heavy shelves
questions.correctAnswer: Drop, cover under a sturdy desk, and hold on until shaking stops
questions.explanation: Covering under sturdy furniture helps reduce injury from falling objects during shaking.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply earthquake safety procedures in school settings.

questions.prompt: Why can earthquakes cause more damage in areas with weak buildings?
options: Weak structures are more likely to crack or collapse during shaking
Weak buildings stop all seismic waves
Earthquakes only occur inside weak buildings
Strong buildings attract earthquakes from far away
questions.correctAnswer: Weak structures are more likely to crack or collapse during shaking
questions.explanation: Damage depends on both earthquake strength and vulnerability of buildings and infrastructure.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain factors influencing earthquake damage.

questions.prompt: A shallow earthquake and a deep earthquake have the same magnitude. Why might the shallow one cause more surface damage?
options: Its energy reaches the surface over a shorter distance
It always produces more rainfall
It has no seismic waves
It occurs only in uninhabited places
questions.correctAnswer: Its energy reaches the surface over a shorter distance
questions.explanation: Shallow earthquakes often produce stronger shaking near the surface than deeper earthquakes of similar magnitude.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze factors that affect earthquake intensity at the surface.

questions.prompt: Which set of observations would help assess earthquake risk in a town?
options: Distance from faults, ground conditions, building quality, and population density
Only the colour of rooftops
Only the number of shops selling food
Only the name of the nearest river
questions.correctAnswer: Distance from faults, ground conditions, building quality, and population density
questions.explanation: Earthquake risk depends on hazard exposure, local ground conditions, vulnerable structures, and people at risk.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze geographical factors affecting earthquake risk.

questions.prompt: Which preparedness plan is best for a school in an earthquake-prone area?
options: Secure heavy furniture, mark evacuation areas, run drills, and keep emergency contacts updated
Lock all emergency exits during lessons
Place heavy shelves above every desk
Avoid teaching learners what to do during shaking
questions.correctAnswer: Secure heavy furniture, mark evacuation areas, run drills, and keep emergency contacts updated
questions.explanation: Preparedness reduces injuries by improving the school environment and rehearsing safe responses.
questions.learningOutcome: Create a practical earthquake preparedness plan for a school.

questions.prompt: Which activity is an example of agriculture?
options: Growing maize and keeping dairy cattle
Extracting soda ash from a lake
Assembling motor vehicles
Selling airtime only
questions.correctAnswer: Growing maize and keeping dairy cattle
questions.explanation: Agriculture involves crop growing, livestock keeping, or related farm production activities.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify agricultural activities.

questions.prompt: Which factor most strongly favours tea growing in Kenya's highland areas?
options: Cool temperatures, reliable rainfall, and well-drained acidic soils
Very low rainfall and salty soils
Permanent snow cover on farms
Flat desert plains with no moisture
questions.correctAnswer: Cool temperatures, reliable rainfall, and well-drained acidic soils
questions.explanation: Tea performs well in cool, wet highlands with suitable soils and good drainage.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe physical factors influencing crop production.

questions.prompt: What is subsistence farming mainly aimed at?
options: Producing food mostly for the farmer's household
Producing only minerals for export
Manufacturing goods in a factory
Generating electricity from steam
questions.correctAnswer: Producing food mostly for the farmer's household
questions.explanation: Subsistence farming focuses mainly on meeting the food needs of the farmer and family.
questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish subsistence farming from commercial farming.

questions.prompt: A farmer plants beans after maize in the same field. Which benefit can crop rotation provide?
options: It can improve soil fertility and reduce pests or diseases
It makes rainfall unnecessary
It turns all soils into rocks
It prevents any need for weeding forever
questions.correctAnswer: It can improve soil fertility and reduce pests or diseases
questions.explanation: Rotating crops can break pest cycles and legumes such as beans may add nitrogen to the soil.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain benefits of sustainable farming practices.

questions.prompt: Which irrigation method delivers water directly near plant roots and reduces wastage?
options: Drip irrigation
Flooding the whole farm every day
Burning crop residues
Deep mining
questions.correctAnswer: Drip irrigation
questions.explanation: Drip irrigation applies water slowly near roots, which can save water in dry areas.
questions.learningOutcome: Select suitable farming technologies for water conservation.

questions.prompt: Which combination best explains why some farms are more productive than others?
options: Climate, soils, farming skills, capital, market access, and transport
Only the colour of the farmer's clothes
Only the month when a farm was named
Distance from the nearest football field only
questions.correctAnswer: Climate, soils, farming skills, capital, market access, and transport
questions.explanation: Agricultural productivity is influenced by both physical and human factors.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze factors influencing agricultural production.

questions.prompt: A semi-arid community wants to reduce crop failure. Which strategy is most suitable?
options: Use drought-tolerant crops, water harvesting, mulching, and timely planting
Grow only water-demanding crops without irrigation
Remove all soil cover before the dry season
Plant crops only on bare rock surfaces
questions.correctAnswer: Use drought-tolerant crops, water harvesting, mulching, and timely planting
questions.explanation: Dryland farming needs practices that conserve moisture and reduce climate risk.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze farming adaptations in semi-arid areas.

questions.prompt: Which plan best supports sustainable agriculture on steep slopes?
options: Terracing, contour farming, grass strips, agroforestry, and controlled grazing
Plough straight down the slope and remove all vegetation
Leave gullies to expand without repair
Cultivate river banks up to the water edge
questions.correctAnswer: Terracing, contour farming, grass strips, agroforestry, and controlled grazing
questions.explanation: Slope conservation reduces runoff, soil erosion, and loss of fertility.
questions.learningOutcome: Develop sustainable soil conservation practices for farming areas.

questions.prompt: Why is transport important for commercial horticulture around Naivasha and other farming areas?
options: Perishable produce needs quick movement to markets and airports
Transport stops crops from ripening on farms
Flowers and vegetables never need markets
Transport changes all crops into minerals
questions.correctAnswer: Perishable produce needs quick movement to markets and airports
questions.explanation: Horticultural products can spoil quickly, so reliable transport supports local and export marketing.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the role of transport and markets in commercial farming.

questions.prompt: What is mining?
options: The extraction of minerals from the Earth
The growing of crops for food
The movement of clouds by wind
The teaching of languages
questions.correctAnswer: The extraction of minerals from the Earth
questions.explanation: Mining involves removing useful minerals from rocks, soils, or other deposits.
questions.learningOutcome: Define mining as an economic activity.

questions.prompt: Which mineral is famously extracted at Lake Magadi?
options: Soda ash
Gold
Diamond
Bauxite
questions.correctAnswer: Soda ash
questions.explanation: Lake Magadi is known for soda ash deposits used in industries such as glass and chemical manufacturing.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify examples of minerals mined in Kenya.

questions.prompt: Why is open-cast mining suitable for some mineral deposits?
options: The mineral lies near the surface and can be reached by removing overburden
The mineral is always found under very deep oceans
The method requires no machinery or labour
The mineral cannot be seen or mapped
questions.correctAnswer: The mineral lies near the surface and can be reached by removing overburden
questions.explanation: Open-cast mining works where deposits are shallow enough to extract from an open pit.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain conditions favouring different mining methods.

questions.prompt: Which economic benefit can mining bring to a local area?
options: Employment, income, infrastructure, and raw materials for industries
Permanent removal of all need for environmental care
Guaranteed equal wealth for every household
Complete absence of land-use conflicts
questions.correctAnswer: Employment, income, infrastructure, and raw materials for industries
questions.explanation: Mining can create jobs and supply raw materials, but it also needs careful management.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain economic contributions of mining.

questions.prompt: Which environmental problem is commonly linked with poorly managed mining?
options: Land degradation, water pollution, dust, and loss of vegetation
Improved soil cover in every mined area
Automatic forest growth without planting
End of all erosion in nearby rivers
questions.correctAnswer: Land degradation, water pollution, dust, and loss of vegetation
questions.explanation: Mining can disturb land and pollute air or water if controls and rehabilitation are weak.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze environmental impacts of mining.

questions.prompt: A company wants to mine near a river used by farmers. Which action should be required before mining begins?
options: Environmental impact assessment and a plan for water protection and land rehabilitation
Immediate excavation without informing affected people
Dumping waste directly into the river
Blocking farmers from reporting pollution
questions.correctAnswer: Environmental impact assessment and a plan for water protection and land rehabilitation
questions.explanation: Mining projects should assess risks and plan safeguards before operations begin.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate responsible mining practices.

questions.prompt: Which post-mining rehabilitation plan is most suitable for an exhausted open pit?
options: Stabilize slopes, refill where possible, replace topsoil, plant vegetation, and monitor water quality
Leave steep loose sides open to erosion
Use the pit for uncontrolled waste dumping
Remove all warning signs and abandon the site
questions.correctAnswer: Stabilize slopes, refill where possible, replace topsoil, plant vegetation, and monitor water quality
questions.explanation: Rehabilitation should make mined land safer, reduce pollution, and support new land use.
questions.learningOutcome: Create a rehabilitation plan for mined land.

questions.prompt: Which energy source is renewable?
options: Solar energy
Coal
Petroleum
Natural gas
questions.correctAnswer: Solar energy
questions.explanation: Solar energy is renewable because sunlight is naturally replenished.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify energy sources as renewable or non-renewable.

questions.prompt: Which Kenyan energy source uses heat from inside the Earth?
options: Geothermal energy
Charcoal only
Imported petrol
Tidal energy from the Rift Valley
questions.correctAnswer: Geothermal energy
questions.explanation: Geothermal power uses underground heat, especially in parts of the Rift Valley such as Olkaria.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify energy resources found in Kenya.

questions.prompt: Why can hydroelectric power generation reduce during a severe drought?
options: Lower river flow reduces the water available to turn turbines
Drought increases river volume everywhere
Turbines only work when rivers are dry
Reservoir levels have no effect on power generation
questions.correctAnswer: Lower river flow reduces the water available to turn turbines
questions.explanation: Hydroelectric power depends on sufficient water flow and reservoir storage.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain how physical conditions affect energy production.

questions.prompt: Which factor makes wind power suitable in some parts of northern Kenya?
options: Strong and reliable winds over open landscapes
Permanent absence of wind
Deep underground coal seams
Very dense forests blocking all air movement
questions.correctAnswer: Strong and reliable winds over open landscapes
questions.explanation: Wind power is best where wind speeds are strong and consistent enough to turn turbines efficiently.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze factors influencing the location of renewable energy projects.

questions.prompt: Which energy plan best improves reliability while reducing environmental harm?
options: Combine geothermal, solar, wind, hydro, efficiency measures, and careful environmental safeguards
Depend on one fuel only and ignore demand management
Cut all electricity supply to reduce planning work
Expand charcoal use without replanting trees
questions.correctAnswer: Combine geothermal, solar, wind, hydro, efficiency measures, and careful environmental safeguards
questions.explanation: A balanced energy mix improves resilience and can reduce pressure on forests and fossil fuels.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate sustainable energy strategies for Kenya.

questions.prompt: What is an industry in Geography?
options: An economic activity that produces, processes, or provides goods and services
A natural lake formed by tectonic movement
A contour line joining equal heights
A seasonal wind direction only
questions.correctAnswer: An economic activity that produces, processes, or provides goods and services
questions.explanation: Industry includes activities such as manufacturing, processing, construction, and service provision.
questions.learningOutcome: Define industry as an economic activity.

questions.prompt: Which factor is most important for locating a sugar factory near cane-growing areas?
options: Sugarcane is bulky and loses quality after harvesting
Sugarcane must be transported for many years before processing
Sugar factories do not need raw materials
Sugarcane grows only inside factories
questions.correctAnswer: Sugarcane is bulky and loses quality after harvesting
questions.explanation: Processing near farms reduces transport cost and loss of quality for bulky, perishable raw materials.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain raw-material influence on industrial location.

questions.prompt: Why are roads, railways, and ports important to manufacturing industries?
options: They help move raw materials to factories and finished goods to markets
They remove the need for workers and energy
They stop all trade between counties
They turn finished goods back into raw materials
questions.correctAnswer: They help move raw materials to factories and finished goods to markets
questions.explanation: Good transport lowers costs and connects industries to suppliers and buyers.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the role of transport in industrial development.

questions.prompt: A town wants to attract light industries without damaging nearby homes and rivers. Which planning approach is best?
options: Zone suitable industrial land, provide waste treatment, improve transport, and monitor pollution
Allow factories to discharge untreated waste into rivers
Place all factories inside residential compounds
Ignore land-use plans and build wherever space appears
questions.correctAnswer: Zone suitable industrial land, provide waste treatment, improve transport, and monitor pollution
questions.explanation: Industrial planning should support jobs while protecting residents, water, and land quality.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze sustainable planning measures for industrial development.
